question: A man worked as a clerk in a gourmet coffee shop. His friend often stopped by the shop to chat with the man while the man was working. not prevail, because the customer should have waited for an employee to operate the machine.
not prevail, because the friend was acting as a Good Samaritan.
not prevail, because the man acted outside the scope of employment by entrusting the supervision of the shop to his friend.
prevail, because the company failed to properly train the man on how to operate the machine.
not prevail, because the friend was not an employee of the coffee shop.
prevail, because the company failed to ensure that the man was never left alone in the shop.
prevail, because the friend's negligence would be imputed to the company.

In terms of negligence law, liability typically extends to actions of an agent or employee within the scope of their employment (vicarious liability). Here, the employee asked his friend to watch the store, and that was not part of his job duties. So the employee was acting outside the scope of employment when he was entrusting the shop to his friend.

Now, could the coffee shop be vicariously liable for the employee's actions? This could happen if the action was authorized by the employer (even if it was a reasonable thing to do). However, asking a friend to watch the store is not part of the standard scope of work, so the employer likely did not authorize this kind of act.
